April 10, 2025
Rethinking California's Reserve Policy
Introduction
Chapter 1: How Much Should the State Save in Reserves?
Chapter 2: Where Are We Now?
Proposition 2 Has Substantially Improved State's Reserve Policy
Yet Further Improvements Are Warranted
Chapter 3: Where Do We Go from Here?
Governor's Proposal
LAO Recommendations
Conclusion
Executive Summary
Rethinking California's Reserve Policy. Reserves allow the state to ensure stable funding for its services over time, even when revenue fluctuates unpredictably. Over the last few years, the state has indeed experienced those significant fluctuations-large surpluses followed by significant deficits. This volatility has prompted interest in changes to the state's reserve policy. The Governor has proposed two changes that, if passed by the Legislature, would go before voters. In this report, we assess those proposed changes. We find that while they would improve upon the state's reserve policy, they would not reliably ensure stable funding for core services over time, and therefore further changes are warranted. As such, we examine how much the state would need to save in reserves to maintain its core services during future downturns.
What Is the Purpose of Reserves? The state will collect more in revenues than the cost of its core service level in some years. In other years, it will collect less. Reserves help smooth the difference-funds are saved when revenues are surging (the green regions in the figure below) and then spent when revenues decline below that long‑term trajectory (the red regions). If reserves are insufficient to cover these shortfalls, the state must eventually: (1) raise taxes or (2) cut those services. This means that the more reserves the state has, the more it can mitigate the need for those cuts and tax increases.
How Do We Evaluate the Performance of Reserve Policies? A reserve policy "performs well" if it meets the central goal of reserves-that is, it allows the state to save enough so that the state can pay for spending on its core services when revenues drop. When revenues are insufficient for the state to pay for its core service level, we describe the difference as a funding shortfall . To evaluate how much funding shortfalls can be covered with reserves we have constructed simulation‑based tools-similar those used in insurance markets and the state's pension system-that use information about the past to forecast many different variations of the future. We report findings across 50 years and thousands of these simulations.
Under Current Law, the State Can Cover One‑Third of Funding Shortfalls. We find that the state's current constitutional rules for building reserves would allow the state to cover about one‑third of funding shortfalls. Put another way, if current law remained in place for the next 50 years, and without further saving above this level, cuts to core services and/or tax increases would often be necessary.
Governor's Proposal Improves Upon Current Law, but Further Improvements Are Warranted. The Governor proposes two changes to the state's reserve policy: (1) raise the cap on constitutional deposits from 10 percent of General Fund taxes to 20 percent, and (2) make reserve deposits excludable from the state appropriations limit. The Governor's proposal improves upon current law-rather than one‑third, these changes would allow the state to cover about half of funding shortfalls over 50 years. However, even with this change, reductions to core services or tax increases would still be common. In our view, this means further improvements are warranted.
LAO Recommended Approach. We put forward two recommendations to improve reserve policy:
Raise the Reserve Cap to 50 Percent by 2055. We first recommend the cap on constitutional reserve deposits be raised from 10 percent to 50 percent of General Fund taxes. The increase could be phased in over time: 20 percent to take effect immediately after the next statewide election, 25 percent in 2030, and increasing by 5 percent every five years until the cap reaches a maximum of 50 percent in 2055.
Two Options to Reach This Higher Threshold. If the cap is raised, the state would also need to set aside more in reserve deposits to dependably reach this higher amount. There are many options for doing this, but given the volatility in the state's revenues, we think it is important to set aside much more funds in years when revenues are surging , rather than setting aside somewhat more in every year. We suggest two alternative mechanisms to accomplish this: (1) create new, more robust and flexible deposit rules, or (2) keep existing rules in place, but change them to set aside more in capital gains revenues in some years.
The figure below shows how the state's reserve policy would perform under our recommended alternatives. As it shows, we estimate our recommendations would allow the state to cover about three‑quarters of funding shortfalls over the next 50 years.
These Recommendations Are an Honest Reflection of Revenue Volatility. We understand that building a reserve of this size-even if achieved over three decades-is a dramatic increase and well outside the range of savings targets that have been contemplated by policymakers to date. Yet we do not view these recommendations as overly cautious-to arrive at these estimates, we have used standard tools from actuaries in pensions and insurance markets. These problems are also clear when California's reserves are compared to other states-California ranks near the top in terms of revenue volatility, but below average in terms of reserves. As such, our recommendations are an honest reflection of the volatility in the state's tax system. That is, these changes would allow the state to enjoy the advantages of its current revenue structure while protecting critical services for Californians for decades to come.
Introduction
Reserves allow the state to ensure stable funding for its services over time, even when revenue fluctuates unpredictably. By setting aside funds when revenues are surging, the state can maintain core services when those revenues fall short. Reserves have become particularly salient to the budget process in recent years. After allocating surpluses totaling over $100 billion across 2021‑22 and 2022‑23, the Legislature has addressed cumulative budget problems of $82 billion in the years since. Budget problems are also likely to persist for the foreseeable future. In fact, given the scale of both actual and projected deficits, the Legislature likely faces the difficult choice about how to reduce core services in the coming years.
In light of these developments, the Legislature has signaled an interest in making changes to the state's reserve policy. In addition, through this year's budget process, the Governor has proposed two changes to the state's rainy day fund that, if passed by the Legislature, would go before voters. This raises an important question: Are these changes sufficient? That is, how much does the state need to save in reserves to maintain its core services during future downturns and would the Governor's proposal achieve that goal? If not, what is a reserve policy that would? This report aims to answer these questions by taking a long‑term view. That is, we aim to construct a reserve policy that has the best chance of withstanding the test of time and minimizes the need for the Legislature to ask voters to make further changes to the Constitution in a few years.
The report is organized as follows. Chapter 1 lays out a framework for establishing a goal for the state's reserve policy, and then tools that can be used to estimate how much in reserves the state needs to save to achieve that goal over time. In Chapter 2, using the tools outlined in Chapter 1, we evaluate the state's current reserve policy. Chapter 3 examines possible changes to the state's policy, including the Governor's proposals and our recommended alternatives.
Chapter 1: How Much Should the State Save in Reserves?
This section presents our framework for thinking about how much in reserves the state should save. First, we describe the goal of reserves. Then, we describe the ways we can quantitatively evaluate whether or not a reserve policy is meeting that goal.
What Is the Purpose of Reserves?
Revenues Are Volatile… From year to year, state revenues can grow very quickly or contract quickly. Revenues drop during economic recessions, when business activity slows, unemployment rises, and consumer spending declines, leading to lower tax collections. Asset market downturns, like stock market drops or real estate slumps, can also reduce capital gains tax revenue and other investment‑related income, lowering state revenue. Conversely, revenues can grow quickly in response to economic expansions or run ups in the stock market.
…And Core Spending Is Not. Meanwhile, the ongoing costs of state programs-the state's core service level-is much steadier. Spending on core services can fluctuate in response to recessions, for example, because of caseload growth in means‑tested programs that occurs in response to unemployment changes. However, in general, growth in core services tracks more stable factors, like inflation (especially inflation for pharmaceuticals and health care) and population (especially in some key demographic areas). Conversely, growth in total spending-rather than spending on core services alone-does fluctuate much more. This is largely because the Legislature allocates considerable shares of revenue surges to one‑time and temporary spending.
Reserves Allow the State to Smooth the Difference. The state will collect more in revenues than the cost of its core service level in some years. In other years, it will collect less. Reserves help smooth the difference. As shown in Figure 1 , reserves can be saved when revenues are surging (the green regions) and then spent when revenues decline below that long‑term trajectory (the red regions). Importantly, this hypothetical-and the estimates of core services in this report-only speak to reserve policy on one side of the budget, that is, excluding the budget devoted to schools and community colleges. The nearby box describes why this is our focus.
Reserve Policy and the Two Sides of the State Budget
State Budget Can Be Thought of in Two Distinct Parts. Functionally, California's General Fund budget is divided into two parts: one dedicated to K‑14 education (about 40 percent of the total) and another part that funds everything else (roughly 60 percent of the total). The reason for this bifurcation is Proposition 98 (1988), which requi res the state to set aside minimum amounts of funding for schools and community colleges. With rare exceptions, the state must fund this baseline regardless of other budget pressures. As a result, Proposition 98 creates a separate budget for K‑14 education that sits within the state's larger budget.
Budget Conditions Can Diverge. The budget situation within Proposition 98 can diverge sharply from the rest of the budget. For example, there can be a "surplus" within the Proposition 98 budget (meaning that funding under the guarantee is more than sufficient to cover the costs of existing educational programs) even as the rest of the General Fund faces a deficit. That said, the conditions of these two parts of the budget tend to move together because, under the constitutional formulas, funding for schools and community colleges will usually decline in response to drops in revenues.
Schools and Community Colleges Have Separate System to Mitigate Revenue Volatility. Revenue volatility is an issue for both sides of the budget, but each side also has distinct and dedicated policies to address that volatility. For schools and community colleges, the main tool is the state's Public School System Stabilization Account (the Proposition 98 Reserve), which requires the state to save more in reserves when revenues-especially those from capital gains taxes-are surging. These funds must be used to supplement, but not supplant, Proposition 98 spending during a downturn. In addition, school and community college districts themselves hold local reserves to manage unexpected cost increases, as well as state funding declines. Finally, the state has used other tools like deferrals, which uses a principle similar to borrowing to help smooth school spending through downturns.
This Report Does Not Address Reserve Policy for Schools. Given the division of the budget and the separate reserve policies in place for schools and community colleges, this report focuses only on the reserve policy for the rest of the budget. That is, the recommendations and estimates in this report only address revenue volatility for the side of the budget that does not include schools and community colleges, and this report does not speak to the adequacy of preparedness for the Proposition 98 budget for revenue downturns.
Reserves Allow the State to Avoid Tax Increases and Cuts to Core Services. The State Constitution requires the Legislature to pass a balanced budget. So, if the state does not have enough reserves to cover shortfalls between revenues and spending on core services, the state must eventually: (1) raise taxes or (2) cut those services. (The state also has the option borrow or shift costs to address deficits, but only on a limited and temporary basis. Functionally, borrowing has the same impact as reserves-it moves money from a period when state revenues are surging to one when they fall short-but generally involves higher interest costs for the state. The main difference, however, between reserves and borrowing is that the former involves setting aside funds up‑front whereas the latter would fund a deficit after the fact.) The more reserves the state has, the more it can mitigate the need for spending cuts or tax increases.
Revenue Downturns Will Occur, the Question Is When. The state's revenue fluctuations are often described in terms of risk, like a car owner protecting against the risk of an accident or a corporation hedging against the risk of changes in sales. A more risk‑averse car owner might purchase full‑coverage insurance while a less risk‑averse car owner might purchase only what is legally required. Yet these analogies do not well describe the state's revenue situation-because , unlike with a car accident, the question of revenue drops is not if but when . That is: the state will face revenue downturns in the future, but we can't predict when those will occur or how big they will be. This makes the state's reserve policy more like an individual saving for retirement. A person saving for retirement does not know how long they will live or exactly what their expenses will be in retirement, but they nonetheless must plan for this eventuality by making the best possible choices in the meantime. That person might experience annual fluctuations in their financial situation that causes them to save more or less in any given year. However, their long‑term plan should be constructed irrespective of these annual fluctuations. This analogy can be easily extended to the state's reserve policy, which can fluctuate from year to year but should be constructed by examining a very long‑time horizon in order to facilitate the stable provision of services.
How Do We Evaluate Reserve Policies?
We Use Simulation‑Based Tools Similar to Those Used to Analyze Pensions and Insurance. The state's reserve policy should hold up not just for a few years or even a couple of decades, but over many economic cycles. In this report, we test reserve policies over 50 years. On an analytical basis, there is nothing inherently correct about this time frame, except that it is long enough to allow us to measure the cumulative effect of several economic cycles. Predicting the exact path revenues will take over the next 50 years is, of course, impossible. However, we can make informed estimates about the future with tools similar those used in insurance markets and the state's pension system. Similar to actuaries in these fields, we have constructed simulation‑based tools that use information about the past to forecast many different variations of the future. With these scenarios in hand, we can then measure how well a reserve policy performs in not just one or two scenarios, but thousands of them.
What Are These Scenarios? Each of these scenarios draws on data from the past-like long‑term growth rates and the stability and the persistence of past trends-to make predictions about the future. However, each individual scenario is also unique. That is, it will look different than the past and all the other scenarios. Some scenarios are unfavorable ones, while others are more favorable (see Figure 2 ). In an unfavorable scenario, for example, the state could face a series of more moderately sized recessions in close proximity to one another. Or, in a very unfavorable scenario, the state could encounter three Great Recessions over the course of five decades. Conversely, in more favorable scenarios, the state might only face a series of mild to moderate recessions, spread far apart over the 50 years.
Choosing the Right Benchmark Scenario. We do not know which of these scenarios will be the state's actual future (or if the future will hold something else, entirely outside of the scope of our scenarios). If the Legislature adopts a reserve policy that performs well in half of scenarios but poorly in the other half (that is, we use the median scenario as a benchmark), it would mean there is something like a coin‑flip chance that the policy would achieve its desired outcomes. It is reasonable therefore to choose a policy that performs well across the substantial majority of scenarios. For our analysis, we use the 90th percentile as our benchmark-that is, we measure the effectiveness of various reserves policies according to how well they do in some of the most unfavorable scenarios, but not the absolute worst. At this level, we can be reasonably confident a particular policy will have its intended impact. Using outcomes from unfavorable scenarios to make policy recommendations is a standard practice for actuaries in fields like pensions and insurance.
How Do We Measure the Core Service Level? In addition

Other Features of Proposition 2
Reserves
 Constitutional Deposits Are Made Into the BSA Until the Balance
Reaches 10 Percent of General Fund Taxes. But discretionary
deposits do not count toward this cap.
 Budget Emergency Required to Suspend Deposits or Make
Withdrawals. Suspending deposits into the BSA or making a

as well as a declaration of a budget emergency by the Governor.

 Deposits Into the BSA Are Included in the State Appropriations

Limit.
Debt
 Extra Debt Payments Are Required Through 2030. After 2030, the
Legislature could choose to continue making debt payments from the
Proposition 2 calculation or deposit the entire amount in the BSA.
 Only Certain Types of Debt Are Eligible. Generally, the remaining

liabilities.

ACA 20
More Reserves and Extra Debt Payments. Assembly Constitutional
Amendment (ACA) 20 would amend the provisions of Proposition 2 to build
more reserves and extend and expand extra debt payments.
Increases the Amount Set Aside When Excess Capital Gains Are
Higher. When excess capital gains exceed 10 percent of General Fund
taxes, 150 percent of that amount would be set aside for reserves and extra
debt payments. (No changes would be made to excess capital gains above
8 percent, but below 10 percent of General Fund taxes.)
Reserves
 Requires Constitutional Deposits Into the BSA Until the Balance
Reaches 20 Percent of General Fund Taxes. Discretionary deposits
would continue not to count toward this cap.
 Changes State Appropriations Limit Treatment for Deposits and
Withdrawals. Deposits into the BSA would be excluded from the
State Appropriations Limit and withdrawals would be included.
Debt
 Extends Required Extra Debt Payments to 2040.
 Expands Eligible Types of Debt. The state could use the
Proposition 2 debt payments to pay current and future Proposition 98

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: October 7, 2026 at 12:59 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 7, 2026 at 1:01 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Placed on the ballot by the California Legislature this summer via Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Proposition 2 asks voters to approve changes to the state budget process. On its face, it doesn’t seem too bad and the title given to it for the ballot is seemingly innocuous, “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.”
As the title and summary suggest, passage of Prop. 2 would double the state budget reserve cap from 10% of General Fund revenues to 20% of General Fund revenues. The General Fund is the state’s main spending account.
Supporters build off the intuition voters may have about the virtues of saving and having a bigger “rainy day fund.” As the author statement in support of ACA 20 argues, “By strengthening California’s Rainy Day Fund, we can protect funding for schools and essential public services, better weather future economic downturns, and leave our children a stronger, more resilient California.”
That argument does key in on a recurring problem facing state government financing, which is its volatility given the state’s heavy reliance on income and capital gains taxes, which are prone to boom and bust cycles. Consistently, the state has succumbed to the temptations of spending more, creating new programs, funding more boondoggles like the California High-Speed Rail project. Then, when the money runs out, the state panics, abruptly slashes some spending and plays budget shell games like borrowing from other state funds to cover General Fund spending.
That gets to the core problem with Prop. 2. The state doesn’t actually have a revenue problem. After accounting for inflation, the state budget has grown 40% since Gov. Gavin Newsom took office. There’s plenty of money coming in. The problem is how the state handles that money, which is irresponsibly.
In 2014, California voters approved another Proposition 2 which built on the state’s reserve rules and required the state to set aside 1.5% of General Fund revenue. Half had to go into the Budget Stabilization Fund, and half toward paying down debt. That latter provision is set to expire in 2030.
Enter the 2026 Prop. 2, which would enable some of the worst behavior of the Legislature, including its practice of borrowing from other state funds, by expanding the types of debts that would count as lawful uses of that money and extending that authorization through 2040.

It’s easy to miss, but the LAO summary of Prop. 2 in the official voter guide mailed out to everyone actually mentions this: “Specifically, these payments could be used to make required payments to schools and community colleges, repay borrowing from other state funds, and repay certain loans from the federal government.” As columnist and editorial board member Susan Shelley notes (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/26/proposition-2-isnt-about-saving-money-its-another-sacramento-shell-game/), “This effectively relieves the state’s General Fund of these IOU payment obligations, freeing up billions of dollars of General Fund revenue for more spending.”
Finally, as noted by Assemblymen David Tangipa and Carl DeMaio, along with Senator Steven Choi, “Prop. 2 creates loopholes and accounting gimmicks so politicians can eliminate any chance of you getting your tax rebate.” What they are referring to is the state constitutional spending cap known as the Gann Limit which, though weakened over the years, requires the state to give rebates to taxpayers under certain circumstances. Prop. 2 makes it harder to ever hit that formula-based limit.
In sum, Prop. 2 operates under the pretense that Sacramento really just wants to become more responsible. What it actually does is further bloat the accounts of the state, enables ongoing budget games and makes it harder for taxpayers to get some of their money back.
Vote no on Prop. 2 and elect more prudent state lawmakers.

Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund.” (Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026). The measure’s own name is the “Save for California’s Future Act.”
Type: Legislatively referred constitutional amendment (a two-thirds vote of each house placed it on the ballot). It will pass with a simple majority.
A vote YES means: California would double the maximum size of its rainy-day fund from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues. It would also capture more money in years when capital-gains revenue spikes, extend mandatory extra debt payments through the 2039–40 fiscal year, and count rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit on state spending in the year the money is withdrawn and spent.
A vote NO means: The current rainy-day fund rules stay in place. The reserve remains capped at 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, and the requirement to split certain deposits between savings and extra debt payments expires after the 2029–30 fiscal year.
Sponsor/proponent: Legislative Democrats and Governor Gavin Newsome. Lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, with support from Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and the governor’s administration.
On the ballot because: The Legislature passed ACA 20 by the required two-thirds margin on June 25, 2026. The Senate vote was twenty-nine to two and the Assembly fifty-nine to eight.
Full legal text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 (2025–2026), California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
LAO analysis: Proposition 2 (2026), Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 2 would enlarge California’s constitutional savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account, better known as the rainy-day fund. That fund already exists. Voters created its current form in 2014, and it is fed by automatic deposits each year. Proposition 2 does not create a new fund. It changes rules that govern how big the fund can grow, how fast it fills during good years, and how long the state keeps paying down old debts alongside it. Notably it also changes how deposits are treated under the Gann limit on state spending.
The headline change is the deposit cap. Today the state must keep making deposits until the rainy-day fund reaches 10 percent of general fund tax revenues. Once it hits that ceiling, extra money that would have gone into savings is instead spent on infrastructure. Proposition 2 raises the ceiling to 20 percent, so the state can keep saving until the fund is roughly twice as large as it can be under current law.
The second change targets boom years. California leans heavily on personal income taxes tied to capital gains, which rise and fall with the stock market. Current law captures capital-gains revenue above 8 percent of general fund tax revenues and steers it into savings and debt paydown. Proposition 2 keeps that trigger and adds a steeper tier on top of it. For the slice of capital-gains revenue above 10 percent of general fund tax revenues, the state would set aside 150 percent of that amount, pulling even more out of the biggest windfalls.
The third change is timing. Under a rule that began in 2015, half of these deposits go into the reserve and the other half pays down long-term debts such as pension and retiree-health obligations. That split is set to expire after the 2029–30 fiscal year. Proposition 2 extends it through the 2039–40 fiscal year. The eligible debts would include current and future school-funding settle-up payments owed under Proposition 98, money the general fund borrows from the state’s own special funds, and the state’s federal unemployment insurance loan, which stands at roughly $20 billion. The last two changes are new. Starting in 2027–28, deposits into the rainy-day fund would count against the state appropriations limit, known as the Gann limit, only when the money is withdrawn. Today they count when deposited.
2. The legal language
Full text: Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, “Save for California’s Future Act,” Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026, California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20)
Key language:
“[T]he amount of a transfer to the Budget Stabilization Account … for any fiscal year shall not exceed an amount that would result in a balance in the account that, when the transfer is made, exceeds 20 percent of the amount of General Fund proceeds of taxes for the fiscal year.” The paragraphs cited are the required transfers, so voluntary deposits fall outside the cap.
On the steeper capture of capital-gains spikes, the amendment directs the state to set aside the sum of “the portion of the estimate … that is in excess of 8 percent, but not in excess of 10 percent” plus “150 percent of the portion of the estimate … in excess of 10 percent” of general fund proceeds of taxes.
On the Gann limit, the amendment provides that starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year, “transfers to the Budget Stabilization Account shall not constitute ‘appropriations subject to limitation’ for purposes of Article XIII B.” Money withdrawn later counts “in the fiscal year in which [it is] withdrawn.”
What it amends: Amends Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the California Constitution, the article that governs state finance and the rainy-day fund. Because it is a constitutional amendment, the legislature cannot repeal or alter it without returning to the voters.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Avelino Valencia and Senators Melissa Hurtado and John Laird, all Democrats, and championed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas with backing from the governor’s administration. It passed the legislature on largely party lines, with only two recorded Senate no votes.
What? Raises the rainy-day deposit cap from 10 percent to 20 percent of general fund tax revenues, captures 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes, extends the required extra debt payments from 2029–30 through 2039–40, and counts rainy-day deposits against the Gann limit only when the money is withdrawn.
Where? Statewide, written into Article XVI of the California Constitution.
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If passed, the new deposit and Gann limit rules would apply starting in the 2027–28 fiscal year and the extended debt-paydown split would run through 2039–40.
Why? Proponents point to California’s volatile, top-heavy revenue base and the recurring deficits that follow every downturn. Their stated goal is to save more in good years so the state can protect schools, healthcare, and public safety without deep cuts or new taxes when revenues fall. The argument against calls the larger fund a “slush fund” and argues that moving deposits outside the Gann limit makes the taxpayer rebates it requires less likely.
4. Trade-offs
California’s revenue system is genuinely volatile, and that volatility is not a matter of opinion. The state relies heavily on personal income taxes from its highest earners, whose incomes rise and fall sharply with capital gains and the stock market. That design produces windfalls in boom years and sudden shortfalls in downturns. Reserves built under the 2014 rainy-day fund measurably softened the blow in the 2020 pandemic recession, and they were drawn down again as the state faced multibillion-dollar deficits in the years since, including an estimated $18 billion gap heading into 2026–27. A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem.
But saving is not free. Every dollar the constitution steers into the reserve or toward extra debt payments is a dollar not available this year for schools, healthcare, child care, or tax relief. Raising the ceiling from 10 to 20 percent and capturing 150 percent of the biggest capital-gains spikes means more revenue is locked away by formula rather than appropriated through the annual budget.
Opponents object because of its effects on the Gann limit. Under the Gann limit, adopted by voters in 1979, revenue above the limit over two years must be split between taxpayer rebates and schools. Rainy-day deposits count as spending under the Gann limit today. Proposition 2 would stop counting them until they are withdrawn, which gives the state more room under the Gann limit in boom years and makes rebates less likely. The state had $27 billion of room under the Gann limit in 2026–27, so the change matters most in years when revenue surges past it.
Two further points deserve consideration. First, a larger cap does not guarantee the money will be there when a recession hits, because the constitution still lets the governor declare a budget emergency and the legislature can suspend or draw down deposits. A bigger fund raises the ceiling on saving, but it does not force the state to keep the money saved. Second, the most concrete and least disputed piece of the measure is the debt-paydown extension. Pension liabilities, retiree health obligations, and federal unemployment-insurance loans are real debts that accrue interest, and paying them down earlier has a measurable, defensible payoff regardless of where one lands on the reserve question. The reserve expansion is the contested part. The debt paydown is the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
A larger reserve gives the state a bigger cushion against California’s well-documented revenue swings, reducing the depth of cuts or the pressure for new taxes in a downturn.
Setting aside 150 percent of the largest capital-gains spikes targets the volatile money that has historically tempted the state into spending commitments it cannot sustain.
Counting deposits against the Gann limit only when they are withdrawn removes a penalty on saving. Under current rules, a deposit uses up room under the Gann limit the same way spending does.
The Legislative Analyst concludes reserves would be higher and that balancing the budget would be “somewhat easier when revenues decline.”
Potential risks
Money constitutionally directed into savings and debt is money not available now for schools, healthcare, and other services, a real opportunity cost in years when the budget is tight.
A higher cap does not lock the money in place. A governor-declared budget emergency still lets the legislature suspend deposits or draw the fund down, so the reserve may not be there when it is needed.
Formula-driven set-asides reduce the legislature’s year-to-year budget flexibility, shifting more spending decisions from elected officials to a constitutional formula.
Excluding deposits from the Gann limit makes its taxpayer rebates less likely in boom years. Withdrawals count when spent, but a surge can sit in reserves past the two-year window that triggers rebates.
The measure does not address the underlying structural imbalance between ongoing commitments and volatile revenues, so it manages the symptoms of volatility rather than the cause.
6. Open questions
How much larger would the reserve actually grow, and how many years of boom revenue would it take to approach the new 20 percent deposit cap?
In an average recession, would a doubled cap meaningfully change how deep the state's cuts have to be, or would the emergency-suspension rules blunt the benefit?
What current programs or tax choices would be crowded out in the near term by steering more revenue into savings and debt paydown?
How much of the extended debt payment would go to new paydown, and how much to settle-up payments and internal loans the state already owes?
In a year when revenue surges past the Gann limit, how much would the state move into the rainy-day fund and holding account, and how much smaller would taxpayer rebates be as a result?
How would the higher reserve interact with the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee and the state’s constitutional spending limit in high-revenue years?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California saves money in good years so it does not have to gut services in bad ones. Proposition 2 would roughly double how much the state can save and pull more from the biggest windfalls. Before you vote, ask whether a bigger locked-away reserve is worth the dollars it takes off the table for schools, healthcare, and other needs today.
A rainy-day fund only helps if the money is still there when the rain comes. This measure raises the ceiling on saving, but the state can still declare an emergency and spend down the fund. Does Proposition 2 build lasting discipline, or does it mostly raise a limit the legislature can waive when it wants to?

The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming? The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%. It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster. Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy. Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty. This voter guide has everything you need to know Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce. “It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure. Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend. “When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican. How long have we had a rainy day fund? Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst. In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund. Sign up for free Δ But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments. In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it. “When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform. The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools. Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years. A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for. Bigger reserve = more to spend? Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending. “The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.” “Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.” In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times. “I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.” READ NEXT What to know about California’s other tax-the-rich measure: Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-3-california/) October 21, 2026 This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. CPC’s 2026 Voter Information Guide
This November, California voters will make choices on a variety of candidates and ballot propositions that could shape the state for years to come.
Our election guide is designed to help Californians make informed decisions by providing an overview of the statewide propositions, the arguments surrounding them, and California Policy Center’s take on the choices facing voters this November.
As a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, CPC does not endorse a particular candidate, party, or ballot measure. CPC recommends that voters independently evaluate the propositions on their ballots to determine what aligns with their own political preferences and values.
Proposition 1 — $11.25 Billion “Veterans” and Affordable Housing Bond Gives Just $1.25 Billion to Veterans
Like Proposition 37 (below), Proposition 1 increases demand for housing without meaningfully increasing the supply of housing. More dollars chasing a constrained housing market will lead to inflation — and make housing even less affordable.
Proposition 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, $10 billion of which would finance affordable housing and homeownership programs. A relatively meager $1.25 billion would be used for farm, home, and mobilehome purchase assistance for some veterans. $1 billion of the borrowed money would go to tribes and housing for farmworkers and college students. The bulk of the money would flow into government programs that subsidize construction and homeownership for a small fraction of Californians, but do little to address the regulatory barriers driving California’s housing shortage. The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates it will cost $500 to $600 million per year for about 25 years to repay the bond.
Supporters argue that several of the state’s affordable housing programs have exhausted their funding and that California has a long history of voters approving similar veterans’ and housing bonds — so why stop spending now? Supporters include Governor Gavin Newsom, the California Democratic Party, the California Housing Consortium, and League of California Cities.
Opponents argue that Proposition 1 uses expensive state borrowing — with principal and interest payments, that initial $11.25 billion we borrow will cost upwards of $25 billion to repay — to subsidize a relatively small number of homes without doing anything to meaningfully expand the supply of housing. Increasing the demand for housing through home ownership assistance without increasing its supply will further drive up the cost of housing in the nation’s most expensive housing markets. Opponents include state Assemblymember David Tangipa and Reform California.
CPC’s Take: NO
Prop. 1 commits California to decades of massive debt payments for piecemeal housing subsidies while leaving the regulatory and development restrictions constraining the state’s housing supply unchanged. Voters concerned about increased government debt, higher taxes and inflation are likely to oppose this measure.
Proposition 2 — Doubles the State’s “Rainy Day Fund” and Lets Sacramento Sidestep Constitutional Spending Limits
Increases the slush fund that Sacramento uses to finance such exotic programs as healthcare for illegal immigrants.
Proposition 2 would raise the cap on the state’s Budget Stabilization Account — commonly called the rainy day fund — from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue. It would also exclude deposits into that account from the state’s constitutional spending limit (known as the Gann Limit, which voters established through Proposition 4 in 1979). This means that, if Proposition 2 is approved by voters, the state will have a larger rainy day fund, and that the Gann limit would not apply to spending from that account.
Supporters argue that a larger reserve helps the state absorb the swings in revenue that come from relying heavily on income and capital-gains taxes paid by high earners. Supporters include Governor Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party.
Opponents argue that the enactment of the Gann Limit was designed specifically to force the government to return excess revenue to taxpayers or schools rather than retain it, and that exempting rainy day deposits from that calculation loosens one of the state’s few constraints on the growth of government spending. Opponents include the California Republican Party, State Assemblyman Joe Patterson and Reform California.
CPC’s Take: NO
“Saving money” always sounds great until you learn that the “savings account” is commonly used to expand government — not to help California weather such unpredictable financial storms as the Great Recession or Covid. In eight years, Gov. Gavin Newsom has nearly doubled state spending. During that time, he dipped into California’s principal rainy-day fund in three fiscal years, withdrawing roughly $20 billion, even as the state maintained multibillion-dollar commitments, such as its expansion of full-scope Medi-Cal to undocumented residents.
Voters who oppose giving Sacramento more ways to sidestep constitutional spending limits are likely to oppose this measure.
Proposition 3 — Makes the “Temporary” Income Tax Hike on High Earners Permanent
An “emergency” tax hike meant to address the emergency of the Great Recession will now become permanent.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the additional income tax on high earners in California that was established by Proposition 30 in 2012, and later extended through Proposition 55 in 2016. The tax is currently set to expire in 2031. The tax applies to single filers earning at least $361,000 and joint filers earning roughly $721,000. Revenue generated by the tax would be split, with 89% allocated to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Supporters argue that making the tax permanent would guarantee schools long-term budget certainty instead of facing recurring expiration fights. The California Teachers Association is a lead supporter of Proposition 3. The California Federation of Teachers, California School Employees Association, and California Democratic Party also support the measure.
Opponents argue that voters were told in 2012 — and again in 2016 — that the tax was temporary, necessary only to help California weather the Great Recession. In that time, it has been one of the factors driving high-income earners to leave California. Ironically, it turns out that raising taxes can actually lower tax revenue. Opponents include the California Taxpayers Association, California Republican Party and Reform California.
CPC’s Take: NO
Proposition 3 is proof of economist Milton Friedman’s observation that “there’s nothing so permanent as a temporary government program.” If you believe that the California Teachers Association and its hundreds of local members need more money to educate far fewer students; that the 40% of the general revenue they are already granted is too modest; and if you aren’t concerned about wealthy Californians departing the state to avoid this tax (as well as the one proposed under Prop. 40), you’ll love this initiative. On the other hand, voters who prioritize tax stability and oppose tax increases are likely to oppose this measure.
Proposition 4 — Allows Public Financing of Election Campaigns
Allows the state and local governments to get into the business of spending taxpayer dollars to fund political activity.
Proposition 4 would allow the state government and local governments to establish programs that provide candidates with public funds under expenditure limits and eligibility criteria. Under current law, public financing of political campaigns for most public offices is prohibited, with the exception of some local offices in charter cities. Proposition 4 would also require state and local governments to establish spending limits and eligibility criteria if they administer these programs. Five California cities — Berkeley, Long Beach, Los Angeles, Oakland, and San Francisco — already operate such programs.
Supporters point to these cities’ programs as evidence the concept is workable. Supporters include the California Democratic Party and ACLU of California.
Opponents argue that people who pay taxes want that money to fund schools, fire departments, libraries, and roads, not political ads and campaigns. Opponents include the California Taxpayers Association, the California Republican Party and Reform California.
CPC’s Take: NO
Voters who prioritize using public tax dollars for essential government services rather than for political campaigns are likely to oppose this measure.
Proposition 5 — Removes Voters’ Right to Choose a Recall Replacement on the Same Ballot
Guts California’s recall process by taking the replacement choice away from voters and shifting control over the vacancy to Sacramento.
Proposition 5 would change how a recalled elected official is replaced. For 115 years, California voters have had the right to recall state officials and, where the recall is successful, to replace those state officials with a candidate chosen by the same voters. Proposition 5 would eliminate the “replace” provision. If Proposition 5 passes, the office of a recalled official would be filled “in accordance with this Constitution and statute” until the next election. In most cases, that means the seat would be filled by the governor’s appointment and legislature’s confirmation. However, in the case of a recalled state legislator, the Legislative Analyst’s Office says that “a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election.” In the case of a recalled governor, the term would be completed by the lieutenant governor. The proposition would also allow the recalled official to run for the office again if a special election is held, but they may not be appointed.
Supporters and the proposition’s authors in the legislature say that the current system gives bad actors an incentive to target officials they disagree with, replacing them with a candidate who may not command majority support in a special election. Supporters include the California Democratic Party, California Common Cause, and League of Women Voters of California.
Opponents argue that the state’s 115-year-old process gives voters an immediate, direct say in choosing a replacement when they vote to remove an official, and that the proposition would hand that power to the political establishment. Opponents include Election Integrity Project California, Inc., the California Republican Party and Reform California.
CPC’s Take: NO
Voters who value public accountability and direct voter control over elected officials are likely to oppose this measure.
Proposition 37 — $25 Billion State-Run Mortgage Finance Experiment
Like Proposition 1, Proposition 37 increases demand for housing without increasing the supply of housing. More dollars chasing a constrained housing market will lead to inflation, making housing less affordable.
Also known as the Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act, this proposition would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a fixed-rate mortgage program for homebuyers. To be eligible, the homebuyer must be a California resident of at least one year, earn no more than 200 percent of the area median income, and provide a three percent or greater down payment. The loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home cost. The proposition stipulates that homes qualified for the program would be newly constructed, or a building repurposed for residential use where the homebuyer is the first residential owner. Buyers would need to secure a first mortgage for the remainder that the program does not cover.
Supporters say the measure will expand the middle-class housing supply and help buyers clear the down-payment hurdle. Supporters include the California Democratic Party and the California Association of Realtors.
Opponents say the government should stay out of the mortgage lending market, and that Proposition 37 will drive up the prices of homes rather than making them more affordable. They also point out the risk that the program’s success is dependent on CalHFA correctly pricing loans to cover its own costs over time. Taxpayer advocates point out that any default on the loan, should the state be unable to pay the bond investors back, would result in California taxpayers being on the hook. Opponents include Reform California.
CPC’s Take: NO
Voters who oppose expanding government intervention into private financial markets are likely to oppose this measure.
Proposition 38 — $8.4 Billion General Fund Debt to Fund Immunology Research
Once more, California government officials think they’re smarter than complex markets.
This initiative would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research, and establish a research institute affiliated with the University of California. At least $4.2 billion would be allocated toward cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. The proposition states that administrative costs would be capped at 2 percent. It also stipulates that the first ten percent of the revenue generated from the research’s results must go to the state’s General Fund until the bond cost is repaid.
Supporters say the measure was designed with fiscal accountability in mind, and point to the potential public-health payoff and public-private partnership. Supporters include the California Democratic Party, the Alzheimer’s Association, and Reform California.
Opponents argue that borrowing (i.e. taking on taxpayer-funded debt) should not fund scientific research, especially because there’s no guarantee that marketable treatments will result. Pharmaceutical companies spend billions on research that goes nowhere in the hunt for drugs that alleviate suffering. California’s history in this sort of practice has been a signal failure — consider 2004 stem cell research which has earned approximately $16 million in revenue from an investment of $6 billion from taxpayers. Because the measure requires any resulting therapies be sold at discounted prices in California, opponents also argue that companies may prioritize selling treatments in other states.
CPC’s Take: NO
Voters who prioritize fiscal discipline and want to limit multi-decade general obligation bond debt are likely to oppose this measure.
Proposition 39 — Voter ID, Citizenship Verification, and Voter Roll Maintenance
Americans are required to show ID to purchase alcohol, to rent a car, to cash a check, pick up a prescription, purchase cigarettes, enter a court house, start a new job, apply for a marriage license, check into a hotel, open a bank account, or buy a gun. Why not require ID to vote?
This measure would require voters to present a government-issued ID for in-person voting (or the last four digits of a government-issued ID to vote by mail). It would also require election officials to maintain “accurate voter registration lists” and report percentages of citizenship-verified voters, and require the State Auditor to audit compliance with these requirements. Currently when registering to vote in California, voters attest to their citizenship under penalty of perjury.

What Would Proposition 2 Not Do?
While Prop. 2 would make a few changes to California’s rainy day fund as well as modestly revise how the Gann Limit works, the measure would largely leave the current rules in place. In addition, Prop. 2 would not touch the state’s constitutional funding requirement for TK-14 schools and community colleges, known as Prop. 98. For example, Prop. 2:
Maintains the requirement to set aside 1.5% of state General Fund tax revenues each year. Half of these revenues would continue to go into the rainy day fund (BSA), and the other half would continue to be used to pay down certain state debts.
Continues to allow state leaders to reduce or suspend deposits into the rainy day fund to address a budget emergency, and maintains the current definition of “emergency.” BSA deposits could continue to be reduced or suspended in the event of a budget emergency, which would continue to be defined as 1) a disaster or extreme peril or 2) insufficient General Fund revenues to meet a prior-year spending level.
Continues to limit the amount of money that may be withdrawn from the rainy day fund to address a budget emergency. State leaders could continue to withdraw only the amount needed to address a budget emergency, and no more than half of the funds could be taken out in the first year of an emergency.
Continues to prohibit state leaders from suspending debt payments to address a budget emergency. State leaders would continue to be prevented from reducing or canceling required debt payments, even if the state faced a disaster or a severe budget shortfall.
Does not make any changes to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee for TK-14 education. Under the state Constitution, the state is required to set aside a portion of revenues for schools and community colleges each year based on various inputs and formulas. Prop. 2 does not make any changes to the formulas or inputs that determine the annual minimum guarantee calculation.
Maintains the current rules for California’s TK-14 education reserve. Prop. 2 does not change the rules governing the PSSSA, the state’s reserve for TK-12 schools and community colleges. For example, all of the conditions required to trigger a deposit into the PSSSA would remain intact. This includes strong capital gains-related income tax revenue, General Fund revenue growth that translates to strong growth in the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee, and no legislative suspension of the guarantee.
Leaves California’s arbitrary spending cap largely untouched. Other than modestly changing the relationship between two state reserves and the Gann Limit, Prop. 2 leaves in place the complex rules that structure California’s spending cap. This cap hinders state leaders’ ability (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/) to respond to the needs of Californians even as these needs have changed dramatically since the Gann Limit was created in 1979.
What Would Proposition 2 Mean for California?
This section explores the implications of several key provisions of Prop. 2, specifically:
Raising the rainy day fund cap to from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenues,
Setting aside more General Fund revenues during “boom” years,
Expanding the types of state debt that may be paid down with set-aside revenues, including unemployment insurance loans and certain TK-14 education obligations, and
Changing the relationship between two state reserves and the state spending cap (the Gann Limit).
This section also considers the implications of maintaining two current rainy day fund provisions that Prop. 2 would leave in place, specifically:
Continuing to prohibit state leaders from reducing or suspending required debt payments during a budget emergency, and
Maintaining the current definition of what qualifies as a budget emergency.
What Are the Implications of Raising the Rainy Day Fund (BSA) Cap to 20% of General Fund Tax Revenues?
Under Prop. 2, the maximum size of the rainy day fund would double, rising from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenues. With a higher cap, the rainy day fund would have the potential to grow substantially larger. This, in turn, would provide a larger “cushion” for the state budget, helping state leaders to better protect vital services when revenues drop during economic downturns and reducing the need for draconian spending cuts that harm Californians.
If the BSA balance were ever to reach the higher 20% cap, the annual General Fund revenues that would otherwise be deposited into the fund (“spillover” revenue) would instead be spent on infrastructure, as under current law. However, with a higher cap, the state would reach the BSA limit less frequently than is currently the case with a 10% cap. Consequently, over time there would be less spillover revenue available for infrastructure investments. On the other hand, the rainy day fund would likely hold a larger balance to help address a budget emergency.

What Are the Implications of Setting Aside More Revenue in “Boom” Years?
Prop. 2 would require the state to set aside more revenue in years when capital gains revenues spike. This change would allow the state to build up the rainy day fund and pay down certain debts faster, reducing future General Fund cost pressures, while modestly curtailing General Fund revenue available for immediate spending needs.
If Prop 2’s “excess” capital gains provisions had been in place between 2010-11 and 2023-24, California would have had to set aside more General Fund revenue in six of those 14 years. This additional set-aside would have amounted to less than 1% or 2% of total General Fund revenue in each of those six years. Capital gains revenue is difficult to project. However, if a similar pattern held going forward, Prop. 2 could take hundreds of millions of dollars — or even more than $1 billion — in revenue “off the table” in some years. This would reduce resources available to address urgent needs that arise, but would also help to pay down additional state debt and further build reserves to address future emergencies.
Although “excess” capital gains revenue, by definition, is not a predictable and reliable revenue source and cannot be counted on to fund ongoing services, it could be reasonable to use it to temporarily meet critical needs. For example, the state could provide more funding for food banks in the wake of federal food assistance cuts, boost support for local governments to address homelessness, and pay child care providers before or at the time of service delivery (rather than after) — a change that would increase providers’ financial solvency.
In certain years, Prop. 2 would modestly reduce revenue that could otherwise be used to support vital services as communities across the state are reeling from deep federal cuts and mounting affordability pressures that are compounding long-standing unmet needs.
However, meaningfully addressing Californians’ needs requires significant and sustained new revenue — well beyond the relatively modest revenue that Prop. 2 would occasionally divert to reserves and debt payments. This underscores the need to reform California’s outdated tax base whether or not voters approve Prop. 2.
What Are the Implications of Expanding the Types of Debt That May Be Paid Down with Set-Aside Revenues?
The state Constitution requires a portion of General Fund revenues to be set aside each year for certain debt payments (unfunded pension and state retiree health liabilities). This requirement cannot be reduced or suspended even in a budget emergency — a provision that Prop. 2 would leave in place. In recent years, for example, roughly $1 billion to $2 billion in General Fund revenues each year remained “off the table” and were not available to support urgent spending needs.
Prop. 2 would broaden the allowable uses of set-aside revenues to include unemployment insurance (UI) debt. If policymakers were to use these debt-paydown funds to repay the principal on the state’s federal UI loans, then a cost currently borne by businesses would be shifted to the state .
Prop. 2 would also allow set-aside revenues to be used to pay down certain obligations related to TK-14 education and Medi-Cal that otherwise would be paid out of the General Fund. If policymakers were to use debt-paydown funds for these purposes, then General Fund revenue would be freed up for other purposes .
However, set-aside revenues are limited. If state leaders were to use more of these debt-paydown funds for the new purposes allowed by Prop. 2, then fewer (or no) funds would be available to reduce unfunded pension and state retiree health liabilities — costs that would eventually be borne by the General Fund.
What Are the Implications of Using Set-Aside Revenues to Repay Unemployment Insurance Loans?
Prop. 2 would allow state leaders to use set-aside revenues for “federal loans made to the Unemployment Fund.” California owes the federal government roughly $20 billion it borrowed to cover the cost of workers’ unemployment insurance (UI) benefits beginning during the COVID-19 pandemic, when unemployment spiked. Using debt-paydown funds to reduce the principal on California’s UI debt would shift a cost currently borne by businesses to the state and do nothing to fix California’s broken UI system.
Shifting a Cost Currently Borne by Businesses to the State
California’s state government is not required to repay the principal on federal UI loans. Instead, federal law requires businesses to repay the principal through automatic increases in their federal payroll taxes. This makes sense: California’s UI debt is the result of a broken system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/revitalizing-unemployment-insurance-in-california/). For decades, state leaders have not required businesses to contribute enough to cover the true cost of the unemployment benefits their workers need.
Using set-aside revenues to repay the principal on California’s UI loans would shift a cost currently covered by businesses to the state. Moreover, this approach would reduce the amount of debt-paydown funds available for other purposes, such as reducing unfunded pension liabilities — costs that would eventually be borne by the General Fund. As a result, to the extent that state leaders were to use set-aside revenues to pay down UI debt, then more General Fund revenue would be needed to reduce other state debts, diverting dollars away from providing services to Californians.
Doing Nothing to Fix California’s Broken UI System
The UI system is chronically underfunded (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/revitalizing-unemployment-insurance-in-california/) because California has failed to modernize the system’s financing to ensure that it generates sufficient revenue to cover the cost of the unemployment benefits workers need.
Consequently, federal loans are expected to become “a permanent feature (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4943)” of the program, with significant implications for the state’s budget. California typically uses General Fund dollars to pay the interest on these loans, which could total around $1 billion annually in the coming years. Using state dollars to pay the interest on UI loans reduces resources that could otherwise be used to address Californians’ affordability challenges or other needs.
Using debt-paydown funds to reduce the principal on California’s UI debt could modestly reduce the state’s annual interest payments in the near term. However, until state leaders address the broken UI financing system, California is expected to remain locked in a perpetual cycle of debt, necessitating ongoing federal loans and putting constant pressure on the state’s General Fund to cover the annual interest owed.
What Are the Implications of Using Set-Aside Revenues to Repay Certain School and Community College (TK-14) Education Obligations?
Prop. 2 would give state leaders a new option to use set-aside revenues to repay certain TK-14 education obligations. Specifically, the measure would allow state leaders to use these funds to 1) cover Prop. 98 “settle up” payments (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5110#Settle_Up), as needed, and 2) more quickly phase out an outstanding debt tied to an accounting maneuver that state leaders adopted in the 2023-24 budget (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) to address an issue related to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. These new options mean that:
State Leaders Could Use Debt-Paydown Funds to Help Address Increases in Prop. 98 Funding Estimates
When state leaders enact a budget, they provide an estimate of the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee for that fiscal year. This initial estimate is updated in subsequent years to reflect changes in revenue estimates and other inputs. The updated inputs sometimes increase the Prop. 98 guarantee, which requires the state to provide additional funding through “settle-up” payments.
The state usually recognizes any increases to the Prop. 98 guarantee in subsequent years and provides the required settle-up payments from the state’s General Fund at that point. In some years, however, settle-up payments have been delayed, most recently for fiscal years 2024-25 and 2025-26, partly due to the state’s limited General Fund capacity to fund that growth.
Prop. 2 would allow set-aside revenues to be used to cover any current or future Prop. 98 settle-up obligations. This change would provide state leaders with an additional funding source for making these payments, which they could use at their discretion, potentially in combination with General Fund dollars. However, using debt-paydown funds for this purpose would compete with other allowable uses, such as prefunding state retiree health benefits.
In addition, using debt-paydown funds to make settle-up payments would not necessarily retire this obligation more quickly. Under current law, there is no required schedule for making settle-up payments, and Prop. 2 does not create one. If set-aside revenues were treated as the sole or primary source for settle-up payments, it could take longer to fully pay down these obligations because the amount of set-aside revenues may not align with the size of the obligation in a given year, especially when state revenues decline and the set-aside shrinks.
State Leaders Could Accelerate the State’s Recognition of $6.2 Billion in TK-14 Costs Incurred in 2022-23
In 2023, tax filing deadlines were extended due to winter storms, and state leaders overestimated the amount of tax revenue that would be received later in the year. As a result, the state provided $6.2 billion more to schools and community colleges than the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee actually required.
State leaders did not reduce the minimum guarantee to account for the lower revenues. Instead, they set up a schedule to recognize those dollars for accounting purposes in future budgets, starting in 2027-28 and ending in 2039-40. The annual cost is $500 million for the first 12 years, with a smaller amount in the 13th year.
Recognizing these costs will directly reduce General Fund revenues that would otherwise be available in those years for state funding priorities outside of the Prop. 98 guarantee. The sooner this $6.2 billion debt is recognized, the sooner the annual General Fund cost ends and those dollars become available for other purposes.
Prop. 2 would allow state leaders to use set-aside revenues to recognize this $6.2 billion debt, which would mitigate the General Fund impact as well as potentially clear the outstanding balance more quickly. However, using debt-paydown funds for this purpose would compete with other allowable uses, such as reducing state retiree pension liabilities.
What Are the Implications of Changing the Relationship Between Reserves and the State Spending Cap (Gann Limit)?
Prop. 2 would allow state policymakers to save more in strong revenue years to better protect vital public services during economic downturns. This is because deposits into two key reserves would no longer count as spending for the purpose of calculations required by California’s spending cap (the Gann Limit). Instead, these deposits would count toward the Gann Limit only when they are withdrawn .
This change would allow state leaders to build up reserves in years when revenues are strong and the state is close to reaching the spending cap, removing a key drawback of the Gann Limit. This change would also modestly increase “room” under the cap by up to a few billion dollars a year, potentially delaying how long it takes for the state to surpass the limit.
These changes are important. The Gann Limit is an arbitrary cap that hinders state leaders’ ability (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/) to respond to the needs of Californians, which have changed dramatically since late 1970s when the cap was established. Meeting the essential needs of residents and building up reserves to address future needs should not be hamstrung by an arbitrary spending cap approved by an earlier generation of voters.
Prop. 2 would allow policymakers to keep the state under the Gann Limit by making deposits into two reserves — the BSA and the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account (“holding account” (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/)). Several factors, including which of these accounts were used for this purpose, would determine when the deposited funds could be withdrawn and how they could be spent. Specifically:
For deposits into the holding account , state law currently requires the funds to be withdrawn within a year — a rule that could be changed by the Legislature.
If withdrawing funds from the holding account would cause the state to exceed the spending cap, then policymakers would lose flexibility over how the funds could be used (their use would be governed by the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)).
Otherwise, if withdrawing the funds would not cause the state to exceed the limit, policymakers would have full control over the funds.
For deposits into the BSA , the portion that was constitutionally required to be deposited could not be withdrawn unless a budget emergency was operative. Any discretionary deposits, on the other hand, could be withdrawn at any time.
If withdrawing funds from the BSA would cause the state to exceed the spending limit, then policymakers would lose flexibility over how the funds could be used (their use would be governed by the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)).
